title: The missing pieces of workflow automation — Shirsha Chaudhuri, Thomson Reuters Labs

summary: Shirsha Chaudhuri from Thomson Reuters Labs delivers a talk on what is missing for AI-driven workflow automation in enterprises. She traces the enterprise AI journey: democratizing generative AI via internal playgrounds (2022-23), moving to RAG and prompt engineering for knowledge tasks, then in 2024 experimenting with agents to automate entire workflows rather than single tasks. The goal is to reimagine business processes, not merely plug AI into existing ones. She presents two illustrative workflows: a customer support pipeline (service desk, RAG-assisted answers, IT ops L2, engineering L3/L4, bug fixes, SLA compliance) and a content creation pipeline (trigger alerts, approvals, research, authoring, editorial reviews, publishing). Both contain many tasks that agents could automate, but Shirsha argues task-by-task automation is not the desired endpoint. She then enumerates nine missing pieces. First, connectors bridging modern agent stacks to legacy IT systems, noting that 71% of Fortune 500 companies still use mainframes and 68% of global IT production workloads run on them. Second, ROI and reliability—stakeholders make binary calls on whether manual labor can truly be eliminated. Third, visionaries—practitioners need domain subject matter experts to co-reimagine processes. Fourth, standardization in how agents are built, packaged, and deployed. Fifth, data and systems—context is fragmented across logs, chat messages, tickets, and siloed systems. Sixth, collaborative UX defining human-agent interaction. Seventh, AI governance translated into different levels of agent architecture. Eighth, control—balancing deterministic and agent-autonomous steps while preserving human oversight. Ninth, agent lifecycle management for ever-changing capabilities. She concludes that the field is at the start of bridging established enterprise technology to agentic workflows.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Enterprise AI evolved from democratizing generative AI (2022-23) through RAG to agent-based workflow automation in 2024, with the next goal being reimagining entire business processes rather than automating individual tasks.
Two common workflows—customer support and content creation—illustrate many automatable tasks but also show that task-by-task automation is insufficient without process-level reimagination.
Connectors to legacy IT systems are a major missing piece; 71% of Fortune 500 companies still use mainframes and 68% of global IT production workloads run on them.
ROI and reliability remain stumbling blocks as stakeholders make binary decisions about whether manual labor can be replaced by agents.
Domain subject matter experts are needed as visionaries to co-reimagine workflows alongside AI practitioners.
Agent standardization—how agents are built, packaged, and deployed—is still lacking in the established tech ecosystem.
Context and data needed by agents are distributed across siloed IT systems, logs, chat messages, and tickets, making correlation across systems a challenge.
Collaborative UX, AI governance translation into agent architecture, human control balance, and agent lifecycle management are additional missing pieces for enterprise agent adoption.

sections.title: Introduction and AI Evolution in Enterprise
sections.summary: Shirsha Chaudhuri introduces herself from Bangalore, working at Thomson Reuters. She traces the enterprise AI journey from democratizing generative AI via internal playgrounds (Open Arena) in 2022-23, through RAG and prompt engineering for knowledge tasks, to the rise of agents in 2024 and the current goal of automating entire workflows and reimagining business processes.

sections.title: Workflow Example: Customer Support
sections.summary: Describes a typical customer support workflow: customer calls service desk, RAG assists with answers, IT ops handles L2 support, engineering handles L3/L4 with observability tools, scripts and tests run, and tickets are updated to meet SLAs. Many tasks are automatable with agents, but the question is whether task-by-task automation is the right approach or if the workflow should be reimagined.

sections.title: Workflow Example: Content Creation
sections.summary: Describes a content creation workflow: alerts/triggers initiate content, approvals enable research, content is created and reviewed by editors, and finalized content goes to publishing teams for formatting and distribution. Again, many tasks are automatable by AI agents, but the question is whether the workflow design itself should change.

sections.title: Missing Pieces for Workflow Reimagination
sections.summary: Enumerates nine missing pieces: (1) connectors to legacy IT systems, citing mainframe prevalence; (2) ROI and reliability concerns from stakeholders; (3) visionaries or domain experts needed to co-reimagine processes; (4) standardization for agent building, packaging, and deployment; (5) data and systems—context is fragmented across silos; (6) collaborative UX for human-agent interaction; (7) AI governance translated into agent architecture levels; (8) control—balancing deterministic and autonomous steps with human oversight; (9) agent lifecycle management for evolving capabilities. Concludes that the field is at the start of bridging established enterprise technology to agentic workflows.
